Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

JERUSALEM (CNN)  -- The international group Human Rights Watch is accusing Israel of firing weapons containing white phosphorus into Gaza. The group demands that the alleged practice cease. Israel is declining to say whether bursts like this over Gaza involve white phosphorus. The group's  researchers in Israel "observed multiple air-bursts of artillery-fired white phosphorus over what appeared to be the Gaza City/Jabaliya area" on Friday and Saturday, the organization said on its Web site. "Israel appeared to be using white phosphorus as an 'obscurant' [a chemical used to hide military operations], a permissible use in principle" under the laws of war, the HRW posting said. "However, white phosphorus has a significant, incidental, incendiary effect that can severely burn people and set structures, fields, and other civilian objects in the vicinity on fire," the posting said. "The potential for harm to civilians is magnified by Gaza's high population density, among the highest in the world." HRW said the use of white phosphorus in Gaza would violate "the requirement under international humanitarian law to take all feasible precautions to avoid civilian injury and loss of life." Last week, an Israel Defense Forces spokesman told CNN: "I can tell you with certainty that white phosphorus is absolutely not being used." Now, however, Israeli officials have a different response to questions about the possible use of phosphorus: "Any munitions that Israel is using are in accordance with international law. Israel does not specify the types of munitions or the types of operations it is conducting." Still, a doctor familiar with the material said it is not possible to tell, based on pictures of burns, whether white phosphorus was responsible. "Dead tissue pretty much looks the same," said Dr. Peter Grossman, president of the Grossman Burn Center in Sherman Oaks, California. The chemical "can burn down houses and cause horrific burns when it touches the skin," said Marc Garlasco, senior military analyst at Human Rights Watch. Since January 3, when Israel began its ground offensive in Gaza, news reports have circulated about the possible use of white phosphorus by the IDF. HRW's assertion was supported by munitions experts and some Palestinian doctors, including Nafiz Abu Sha'aban, who said the burns it caused were unlike anything he has seen in 27 years of practice. Watch footage of burn patients in Gaza . Though most severely burned patients have been sent to Egypt, the ongoing fighting has made it impossible to evacuate all of them, including one man with deep burns over 47 percent of his body, the doctor said. White phosphorus is known to burn flesh down to the bone. It's intended to provide illumination or to create a smokescreen in battle. Under an international protocol ratified by Israel in 1995, the use of such incendiary weapons is allowed when "not specifically designed to cause burn injury to persons." There is no prohibition per se against white phosphorus in conflict. But the timing and location of its use are restricted. For example, it is illegal under the protocol to use white phosphorus against any personnel, civilian or military. It can be directed only against military targets. International law says incendiary weapons cannot be used where civilians are concentrated. A house north of Gaza City was hit Sunday by something that observers contend may have been white phosphorus. "It's been burning since one o'clock in the morning," Munir Hammada told CNN 11 hours later. "If you move it with your feet, it reignites. You can't put it out with water, only sand." Those characteristics match the properties of white phosphorus, which ignites on contact with air.

JERUSALEM (CNN) — Human Rights Watch, the international advocacy organization, has alleged that Israel fired munitions containing white phosphorus into Gaza and has called for the reported practice to stop.

Israel has not confirmed whether explosions seen over Gaza involved white phosphorus. In a statement posted on its Web site, Human Rights Watch said its researchers in Israel saw “multiple air-bursts” of artillery-fired white phosphorus on Friday and Saturday over an area that appeared to include Gaza City and Jabaliya.

According to the organization, Israel seemed to be using the substance as an “obscurant,” meaning a chemical agent used to conceal military activity. Human Rights Watch noted that such a use can, in principle, be permitted under the laws of war. However, the group warned that white phosphorus also has a major incidental incendiary effect: it can cause severe burns and ignite buildings, fields and other civilian property nearby.

The organization said the danger to civilians is especially serious in Gaza because of its extremely dense population, which is among the highest in the world. Human Rights Watch argued that using white phosphorus in Gaza would breach the obligation under international humanitarian law to take every feasible step to prevent civilian deaths and injuries.

The previous week, an Israel Defense Forces spokesman told CNN, “I can tell you with certainty that white phosphorus is absolutely not being used.” Israeli officials are now answering questions differently, saying that all munitions used by Israel comply with international law and that Israel does not disclose the specific weapons or operations it employs.

A physician familiar with burn injuries cautioned that photographs alone cannot prove whether white phosphorus caused particular wounds. “Dead tissue pretty much looks the same,” said Dr. Peter Grossman, president of the Grossman Burn Center in Sherman Oaks, California.

Marc Garlasco, Human Rights Watch’s senior military analyst, said white phosphorus “can burn down houses and cause horrific burns when it touches the skin.”

Since Israel launched its ground operation in Gaza on January 3, reports have emerged suggesting that the Israel Defense Forces may have used white phosphorus. Human Rights Watch’s claim has been backed by munitions specialists and some Palestinian doctors, including Nafiz Abu Sha’aban, who said the burns he had seen were unlike any injuries he had encountered in 27 years of medical practice. Footage showed burn patients in Gaza.

Most patients with the worst burns have been transferred to Egypt, but continuing combat has prevented all of them from being evacuated, Abu Sha’aban said. One patient, he added, had deep burns covering 47 percent of his body.

White phosphorus is known for its ability to burn human tissue down to the bone. Militarily, it is used to illuminate areas or produce a smoke screen during combat. Under an international protocol that Israel ratified in 1995, incendiary weapons may be used if they are “not specifically designed to cause burn injury to persons.”

White phosphorus itself is not categorically banned in war, but international rules restrict when and where it may be used. Under the protocol, it is unlawful to use white phosphorus against people, whether civilians or military personnel. It may be used only against military objectives. International law also bars incendiary weapons from being used in areas where civilians are concentrated.

On Sunday, a home north of Gaza City was struck by something that observers said may have been white phosphorus. “It’s been burning since one o’clock in the morning,” Munir Hammada told CNN 11 hours afterward. “If you move it with your feet, it reignites. You can’t put it out with water, only sand.”

Those details are consistent with white phosphorus, which catches fire when exposed to air.

counterfactuals.output:
**Jerusalem** — Human Rights Watch has accused Israel of using white phosphorus munitions in military operations in Gaza, saying the weapon poses a grave risk to civilians in the densely populated enclave, while Israel’s military has said it complies with international law and has disputed allegations of unlawful use.

In a report and accompanying statements, the rights group said it verified videos and witness accounts that it says show airburst white phosphorus artillery shells used over the Gaza port and other populated areas during Israel’s military campaign against Hamas. Human Rights Watch said the use of such munitions in crowded civilian areas could cause severe burns and long-term suffering, and may violate international humanitarian law.

White phosphorus is a chemical substance that ignites when exposed to oxygen, creating intense heat and thick smoke. Militaries commonly use it to create smoke screens, mark targets or illuminate battlefields. It is not banned outright under international law, but its use is restricted, particularly when deployed in ways that endanger civilians.

The Israel Defense Forces has previously said it uses weapons in accordance with international law and takes feasible precautions to minimize civilian harm. Israeli officials have also said Hamas embeds its fighters and military infrastructure in civilian neighborhoods, including near homes, schools, mosques and hospitals — an allegation Hamas denies.

Asked about allegations involving white phosphorus, the IDF has in past statements said it is “not aware” of the use of such munitions in Gaza or that it uses them only in accordance with legal requirements. Israel has also rejected accusations that it intentionally targets civilians, saying its strikes are aimed at Hamas following the militant group’s October 7 attacks in Israel.

Human Rights Watch said its findings were based on interviews with witnesses, analysis of photos and videos, and the identification of artillery-fired white phosphorus projectiles. The organization said the apparent use of airburst munitions was especially concerning because burning fragments can spread over a wide area, increasing the likelihood of civilian casualties.

Medical experts say white phosphorus injuries can be devastating. The substance can burn through skin and tissue, reignite when exposed to air, and cause organ damage if absorbed into the body. Doctors who have treated such injuries say removing phosphorus particles can be difficult and dangerous, requiring specialized care that may be scarce in Gaza’s overwhelmed health system.

“White phosphorus burns are among the most severe and complex injuries a trauma team can face,” one emergency medicine specialist familiar with conflict-related burns said. “They can continue burning until deprived of oxygen, and patients may suffer both deep tissue damage and systemic poisoning.”

Palestinian witnesses in Gaza have described seeing bright streaks in the sky followed by falling sparks and a choking smell. Some residents said they fled homes or shelters after smoke filled streets and buildings. One man in Gaza City told rights researchers that “pieces of fire” fell near his neighborhood and that people were afraid to step outside because the burning material appeared to scatter across rooftops and roads.

CNN and other news organizations have previously documented civilian accounts of intense bombardment in Gaza, though independent verification of specific munitions in active combat zones is often difficult. Access to Gaza for international journalists and investigators has been severely restricted, and communications blackouts and insecurity have complicated efforts to confirm events on the ground.

Under international humanitarian law, parties to a conflict must distinguish between combatants and civilians and may not carry out attacks that are indiscriminate or disproportionate. Incendiary weapons are specifically addressed under Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which restricts their use in concentrations of civilians. Israel is not a party to Protocol III, but it remains bound by broader customary rules of war requiring civilian protection.

Human Rights Watch has called on Israel to stop using white phosphorus in populated areas and to use less harmful alternatives for smoke screening. The group has also urged the United States and other countries to scrutinize arms transfers and press for accountability where weapons may have been used unlawfully.

Israel has faced growing international criticism over the scale of destruction and civilian casualties in Gaza, where local health authorities have reported thousands killed since the start of the war. Israel says its campaign is necessary to dismantle Hamas after the group’s attacks killed around 1,200 people in Israel and saw more than 250 others taken hostage, according to Israeli authorities.

The dispute over white phosphorus adds to mounting legal and diplomatic scrutiny of the conduct of the war, as humanitarian organizations warn that civilians trapped in Gaza remain at extreme risk from bombardment, displacement, shortages of medical supplies and the collapse of basic services.

**Report: Allegations of Israeli White Phosphorus Use in Gaza During 2009 War Raised Legal and Medical Concerns**

**Gaza/Jerusalem —** Allegations that the Israel Defense Forces fired white phosphorus artillery shells over densely populated areas of the Gaza Strip during the 2008–2009 conflict have drawn sustained scrutiny from human rights investigators, doctors, munitions specialists and international humanitarian law experts.

Human Rights Watch, in a major report released after the fighting, alleged that Israeli forces repeatedly air-burst white phosphorus munitions over civilian areas during “Operation Cast Lead,” the three-week conflict between Israel and Hamas that began in late December 2008 and ended in January 2009. The group said the use of the substance in crowded neighborhoods caused civilian casualties and damaged civilian infrastructure, including homes, medical facilities and a United Nations compound.

White phosphorus is a chemical substance used in military shells to create smoke screens, mark targets or illuminate areas. It ignites on contact with oxygen and burns at extremely high temperatures. While it is not banned outright under international law when used for legitimate military purposes, its use in or near civilian concentrations is highly controversial because burning fragments can spread over a wide area and cause severe injuries.

## Human Rights Watch Findings

Human Rights Watch said its researchers found evidence that Israeli forces used 155mm artillery shells containing white phosphorus in populated parts of Gaza. The organization identified shell remnants and interviewed witnesses, medical personnel and victims.

In its report, **“Rain of Fire: Israel’s Unlawful Use of White Phosphorus in Gaza,”** Human Rights Watch alleged that Israeli forces fired white phosphorus shells in a manner that “unnecessarily and unlawfully” put civilians at risk. The group said the shells appeared to have been air-burst, dispersing burning wedges of phosphorus over broad areas.

Human Rights Watch said it documented cases in which white phosphorus struck or landed near civilian sites, including residential areas and humanitarian facilities. Among the incidents cited by investigators was the shelling near the **United Nations Relief and Works Agency compound in Gaza City** in January 2009, where fires destroyed or damaged humanitarian supplies. The group also examined incidents involving civilian homes and areas around hospitals.

The organization argued that even if the munitions were used to create smoke screens, their deployment over densely populated neighborhoods was inconsistent with the obligation to take all feasible precautions to minimize harm to civilians.

## Doctors Report Severe Burns

Doctors who treated casualties in Gaza during the conflict reported injuries consistent with white phosphorus exposure. Medical personnel described deep thermal and chemical burns that continued to smoke or reignite when exposed to air, a characteristic associated with white phosphorus.

Physicians at Gaza hospitals told investigators and journalists at the time that some patients arrived with burns that were difficult to extinguish and that penetrated deeply into tissue. In severe cases, white phosphorus can burn through skin and muscle to the bone. It can also cause systemic poisoning if absorbed into the body.

Doctors also reported difficulties treating such injuries in Gaza’s overstretched hospitals, which were coping with large numbers of trauma patients amid shortages of medical supplies and disruptions caused by the fighting.

Medical experts have noted that white phosphorus wounds require specialized treatment: fragments must be removed, burns must be kept wet or deprived of oxygen to prevent reignition, and clinicians must monitor patients for organ damage and electrolyte disturbances.

## Munitions Experts Identify Shells

Munitions experts who reviewed photographs, videos and physical remnants from Gaza identified markings consistent with U.S.-made **M825A1 155mm white phosphorus artillery shells**, a type designed to disperse phosphorus-impregnated felt wedges in the air.

Human Rights Watch and other investigators reported finding shell casings and canisters bearing markings associated with white phosphorus rounds. The M825A1 shell typically functions by bursting in the air and scattering burning material over an area that can extend hundreds of meters, depending on altitude, wind and firing conditions.

Experts said such shells can be lawful when used in open areas to obscure troop movements or mark locations, but are highly dangerous in urban settings because the burning fragments cannot be precisely controlled after dispersal.

## Israel’s Position

Israeli officials initially defended the IDF’s conduct, saying the military used weapons in accordance with international law and that Hamas fighters operated from civilian areas, creating complex battlefield conditions. Israel has long argued that Hamas’s use of rockets, tunnels and positions near civilian infrastructure placed Israeli forces and Palestinian civilians at risk.

Following international criticism, Israel conducted internal inquiries into the use of white phosphorus. Israeli authorities acknowledged the use of smoke munitions containing white phosphorus during the conflict but rejected claims that the use was deliberately aimed at civilians.

Israel later said it had taken disciplinary action in connection with at least one incident involving white phosphorus, though human rights organizations criticized the measures as inadequate and called for independent investigations.

## International Humanitarian Law

Under international humanitarian law, parties to a conflict must distinguish between combatants and civilians and between military objectives and civilian objects. They must also avoid indiscriminate attacks and refrain from attacks expected to cause civilian harm excessive in relation to the anticipated military advantage.

White phosphorus is not prohibited in all circumstances. It is not classified simply as a chemical weapon when used for smoke, illumination or marking rather than as a poison. However, its effects can make its use unlawful if employed indiscriminately or without adequate precautions in civilian areas.

Legal experts have pointed to several relevant principles:

- **Distinction:** Attacks must be directed at military targets, not civilians.
- **Proportionality:** Expected civilian harm must not be excessive compared with the concrete military advantage anticipated.
- **Precautions:** Forces must take all feasible steps to avoid or minimize civilian casualties.
- **Incendiary weapons rules:** Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons restricts the use of incendiary weapons in concentrations of civilians. There is debate over whether white phosphorus used primarily for smoke falls within the protocol’s definition, but humanitarian law principles still apply regardless.

Human Rights Watch argued that the IDF’s alleged use of air-burst white phosphorus over crowded Gaza neighborhoods violated these principles because safer alternatives for smoke screening were available and because the risks to civilians were foreseeable.

## Broader Context

The 2009 Gaza conflict, known in Israel as **Operation Cast Lead**, resulted in heavy Palestinian casualties and widespread destruction in Gaza, while Israeli communities faced rocket fire from Palestinian armed groups. The fighting triggered multiple investigations by human rights organizations and international bodies into alleged violations by both Israeli forces and Palestinian armed groups.

The allegations concerning white phosphorus became one of the most prominent controversies of the war because of the weapon’s visible effects and the severity of reported injuries. Images of burning fragments falling over Gaza and fires at civilian sites intensified calls for accountability.

Human rights organizations urged Israel to stop using white phosphorus artillery shells in populated areas and to conduct credible investigations. They also called on Palestinian armed groups to cease indiscriminate rocket attacks against Israeli civilians, which are unlawful under international humanitarian law.

## Continuing Significance

The 2009 allegations remain a reference point in debates over the use of explosive and incendiary weapons in urban warfare. Military lawyers and humanitarian organizations continue to cite Gaza as an example of the legal and ethical dangers posed by area-effect munitions in densely populated environments.

While white phosphorus remains a lawful munition in some military contexts, doctors, weapons experts and rights advocates say its use near civilians carries an exceptionally high risk of severe burns, fires and long-term suffering. The central legal question is not merely whether white phosphorus was used, but whether it was used in a manner consistent with the laws of war.

Doctors in Gaza have described treating patients with unusually deep burns that they said were difficult to manage amid the collapse of medical services. Burn specialists say white phosphorus injuries can be especially dangerous because particles can embed in the skin, continue reacting with oxygen, and cause damage to tissue and organs.

Palestinian physicians have reported cases in which wounds appeared to smoke or reignite during treatment, a phenomenon consistent with white phosphorus exposure, according to burn experts. Medical workers say they have struggled to treat such injuries because hospitals are short of water, dressings, pain medication and surgical supplies.

Civilians in affected neighborhoods have also described fires that were hard to extinguish. Some residents said material falling from the sky set homes, clothing and bedding alight, and that flames would flare again after being doused.

One displaced resident described seeing “sparks” fall across a residential area, followed by fires spreading through rooms and courtyards. Others said they feared returning to damaged homes because debris appeared capable of reigniting when disturbed.

Humanitarian groups say the risks are magnified in Gaza, where large numbers of civilians have been sheltering in overcrowded areas with limited access to emergency services. Firefighting crews have been hampered by fuel shortages, damaged roads and continued bombardment.

International law requires parties to a conflict to distinguish between combatants and civilians and to avoid weapons or tactics likely to cause disproportionate civilian harm. Rights groups have called for investigations into reported use of incendiary munitions in populated areas and for the preservation of evidence.

Israel has repeatedly accused Hamas of operating from civilian neighborhoods, hospitals and schools, saying this places civilians at risk. Hamas has denied using civilians as human shields.

As the war continues, doctors and aid workers say identifying the precise cause of burns is difficult without laboratory testing, access to munition remnants and independent investigators on the ground. But they warn that the injuries and fire patterns described by witnesses demand urgent scrutiny.

“Whatever the munition, the result for civilians is devastating,” one Gaza physician said, describing patients arriving with severe burns at hospitals already overwhelmed by trauma cases. “We are treating wounds we do not have the supplies to treat.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a long-form breaking news piece from Jerusalem about controversy over Israel’s alleged use of white phosphorus in Gaza, explaining what the chemical does, whether it is legal, and why rights groups say civilians are at risk.
counterfactuals.output:
**JERUSALEM —** A widening controversy over Israel’s alleged use of white phosphorus in Gaza has intensified scrutiny of the conduct of the war in one of the world’s most densely populated territories, with human rights groups warning that the substance can cause severe burns, ignite homes and endanger civilians when used in built-up areas.

The Israeli military has faced repeated allegations from rights organizations and researchers that it has fired artillery shells containing white phosphorus during operations in or near Gaza. Israel has said its forces operate in accordance with international law and has previously described white phosphorus munitions as being used for lawful purposes such as creating smoke screens, not as weapons directed at civilians.

The dispute has become a flashpoint in a broader debate over battlefield tactics in Gaza, where Palestinian civilians have had limited ability to flee bombardment and where hospitals, shelters and residential neighborhoods are often packed with displaced families.

## What is white phosphorus?

White phosphorus is a wax-like chemical substance that ignites when exposed to oxygen. Once burning, it can produce intense heat and thick white smoke. Militaries use it most commonly to obscure troop movements, mark targets or create smoke screens.

But it is also dangerous. Burning white phosphorus can reach extremely high temperatures and can continue to burn until deprived of oxygen. If particles land on skin, they can cause deep thermal and chemical burns, sometimes down to the bone. The substance can reignite when bandages are removed or when exposed again to air. Inhalation of smoke can also harm the respiratory system, and fires started by falling particles can spread rapidly in civilian areas.

Doctors and weapons experts say injuries from white phosphorus are particularly difficult to treat because fragments can remain embedded in tissue. Exposure can also cause organ damage in severe cases.

## Is it illegal?

White phosphorus is not banned outright under international law. Its legality depends largely on how and where it is used.

Using white phosphorus to create smoke, illuminate an area or mark a position may be lawful in military operations. However, international humanitarian law requires all parties to a conflict to distinguish between combatants and civilians, avoid indiscriminate attacks, take precautions to minimize civilian harm and refrain from attacks where expected civilian damage would be excessive in relation to the anticipated military advantage.

The controversy is sharpest when white phosphorus is used in or near populated areas. Rights groups argue that air-bursting shells over dense neighborhoods can scatter burning fragments over a wide radius, making it impossible to control where they land. That, they say, creates an unacceptable risk of civilian casualties and fires.

There is also a treaty known as Protocol III of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons, which restricts the use of incendiary weapons in concentrations of civilians. The legal analysis can be complicated because some militaries classify white phosphorus munitions primarily as smoke-producing rather than incendiary weapons, depending on their intended use. Humanitarian groups have long argued that this distinction creates a loophole because the substance’s incendiary effects are the same for civilians on the ground.

## Why rights groups are raising alarms

Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and other organizations have previously accused Israel of using white phosphorus in Gaza and Lebanon, citing videos, witness accounts, photographs and remnants of artillery shells. They argue that using the substance in Gaza is especially hazardous because of the territory’s population density, the destruction of infrastructure and the large number of displaced civilians sheltering in schools, hospitals and apartment blocks.

Rights groups say the main danger is not only direct injury from burning particles but also secondary fires. In Gaza, where many people have been living in damaged buildings, tents or crowded shelters, falling white phosphorus can ignite bedding, clothing, plastic sheeting, fuel supplies and debris. Limited access to water, overwhelmed emergency services and damaged roads can make fires harder to extinguish and burns harder to treat.

Medical care is another concern. Gaza’s hospitals have been under severe strain, with shortages of medicine, fuel, surgical supplies and specialized burn treatment. White phosphorus injuries can require intensive, repeated procedures, and doctors may need training and equipment to safely remove particles from wounds.

“Even if white phosphorus is intended as a smoke screen, its use over crowded civilian areas poses grave risks,” rights advocates have argued. They say militaries should use safer alternatives when operating near civilians.

## Israel’s position

Israel has generally maintained that its military actions comply with international law and that it does not deliberately target civilians. Israeli officials have said Hamas and other armed groups operate from within civilian areas, making military operations more complex. The Israel Defense Forces have previously stated that munitions are used according to legal guidelines and operational necessity.

In past conflicts, Israel has faced criticism over white phosphorus use, including during the 2008-09 Gaza war. After international outcry, Israel said it would restrict or alter its use of some white phosphorus munitions in populated areas. Rights groups say later incidents show the issue has not gone away.

The Israeli military has not always confirmed specific munitions use in real time, and battlefield claims are often difficult to verify independently because access to Gaza is restricted and conditions are dangerous.

## Why Gaza makes the issue especially sensitive

Gaza is a narrow coastal enclave with more than two million people, many of whom have been displaced during the war. Large areas have been heavily damaged, and civilians often move repeatedly in search of safety. In such an environment, weapons that spread burning material across a broad area are particularly controversial.

International law does not prohibit all civilian casualties in war, but it does prohibit indiscriminate attacks and requires precautions to reduce harm. The central question in the white phosphorus debate is whether its use in Gaza can be controlled enough to meet those obligations.

Weapons experts say artillery-fired white phosphorus is especially problematic in urban settings because shells can burst in the air and disperse felt wedges or fragments soaked in the chemical over a large footprint. Wind can carry smoke and particles beyond the intended area. If used close to civilians, schools, hospitals or shelters, the risk increases.

## What investigators look for

To assess allegations, investigators typically examine videos of distinctive smoke trails, satellite imagery, munition remnants, impact patterns, medical reports and witness testimony. White phosphorus shells often produce thick white smoke and multiple descending streaks of burning material. Analysts may also identify markings on shell casings or fragments.

However, confirming use and determining whether it violated the law are separate questions. Investigators would need to establish the location, timing, munition type, intended military purpose, proximity to civilians and precautions taken.

## The broader stakes

The controversy has added pressure on Israel from international rights organizations, humanitarian agencies and some foreign governments already concerned about civilian casualties in Gaza. It has also renewed calls for clearer restrictions on white phosphorus and other incendiary weapons in populated areas.

For Palestinians in Gaza, the allegations deepen fears about the weapons being used around them. For Israel, the issue intersects with its argument that it is fighting an enemy embedded in civilian infrastructure while trying to preserve operational flexibility.

The legal and moral question now facing investigators and governments is not simply whether white phosphorus was used, but whether it was used in a way that put civilians at unlawful risk.

As the war continues and access to Gaza remains limited, the controversy is likely to persist — fueled by new footage, battlefield remnants and the testimony of civilians and doctors confronting the consequences of weapons whose effects can linger long after the smoke clears.
